title: Favourite-longshot bias (cross-sport)
mechanism: Recreational bettors overbet longshots relative to their true win probability (risk-seeking on long odds, availability/salience of big payouts) and underbet heavy favourites, so bookmakers can shade prices toward favourites and still clear the book; net effect is favourites outperform their implied probability and longshots underperform.
claimed_edge: Newall and Cortis (2021) literature review of favourite-longshot bias studies across sports finds the bias is a frequent but inconsistent finding; direction and size vary by sport and era, and several studies find a reverse (favourite-side) bias instead, so no single universal edge size is supportable from the review.
data_needed: Full odds-to-outcome calibration curve (implied probability vs realized win rate) by odds bucket, by sport and season, at both opening and closing lines.
skeptic_note: The review itself is the skeptic: it finds the literature split between favourite-longshot and reverse-favourite-longshot results depending on sport, market type (parimutuel vs fixed-odds vs exchange) and period, so citing it as a usable edge in any one sport without sport-specific recent data is not supportable.

title: MLB favourite-longshot bias vanishes by closing odds
mechanism: Opening moneylines are set before most public money arrives and before late injury/lineup news, so they still carry the bookmakers prior plus any residual favourite-longshot misperception; by closing time, sharp money and full information have moved the price, arbitraging the bias away.
claimed_edge: A Harvard thesis (Swing and a Miss: Uncovering Behavioral Biases in MLB Betting Markets), using 2010-2021 MLB moneyline data, reports the favourite-longshot bias is clearly present in opening odds but disappears in closing odds, with the effect stronger in home games.
data_needed: Paired opening and closing MLB moneylines (home and away) for every regular-season game 2010 onward, plus final scores to compute realized win rates by odds bucket.
skeptic_note: This is itself a built-in refutation of the opening-line edge: the thesis own result says the bias is gone by the close, so it is not actionable for anyone betting at or near closing lines, which is the relevant price for this project; it would only matter for someone who can transact at the open.

title: NFL late-season home-underdog bias
mechanism: Borghesi argues the market overprices favourites in general, but this overpricing is concentrated almost entirely in weeks 15 and later, when bettor and bookmaker attention shifts to playoff races and public money piles onto playoff-relevant favourites, leaving home underdogs in that late window underpriced relative to their true cover probability.
claimed_edge: Borghesi (2007, Applied Economics), The late-season bias: explaining the NFLs home-underdog effect, finds the aggregate home-underdog advantage documented in earlier NFL literature (home underdogs historically covering at rates above 50 percent, with older samples such as 1973-1979 near 58 percent) is driven almost exclusively by week-15-onward games rather than being spread evenly across the season.
data_needed: Spread line, week number, home/away moneyline or spread side, and ATS result for every NFL regular-season game, split into weeks 1-14 vs weeks 15+.
skeptic_note: Search evidence also shows the raw home-underdog win rate has been declining decade over decade (58.1 percent in 1973-1979, down to roughly 52-54 percent by the 2000s-2010s), and separately that NFL home-field advantage itself has been shrinking or disappearing since 2019-2023 for reasons unrelated to betting markets (rule changes, fewer true road disadvantages); either trend would shrink or erase this effect in our 2006-2019 sample, so it must be tested on the actual data rather than assumed.

title: NFL letdown bias after clinching a playoff spot
mechanism: Once a team has clinched a playoff seed, bettors anchor on that teams season-long strong play and bookmakers set opening lines using recent form and season-long rating, both of which ignore the drop in motivation and starter-rest in games that no longer matter for seeding; this is framed as an anchoring plus affect (motivation-blindness) story.
claimed_edge: A Financial Services Review paper, Anchoring, affect, and efficiency of sports gaming markets around playoff positioning, reports opening lines are biased toward teams that have clinched a playoff position, creating a profitable fade-the-clinched-team opportunity; closing lines move toward efficiency and shrink the edge, but betting against teams that clinched a top seed specifically remains statistically and economically profitable even after paying standard commission.
data_needed: Weekly division/conference standings and playoff-clinching status (clinched any berth, clinched a top seed, eliminated) for every team-week, joined to opening and closing spreads and ATS results for the relevant late-season games.
skeptic_note: The paper itself reports the edge shrinks substantially from open to close and survives, by their account, only for the narrow top-seed-clinched subset; that is a small, late-season-only sample per year, so statistical power is inherently low and the result needs replication outside the original sample before treating it as live.

title: NFL point-spread overreaction and recency bias
mechanism: Bettors and, to a lesser extent, line-setters overweight a teams most recent one to five games relative to its true underlying ability (a representativeness/recency heuristic), pushing the spread too far toward teams coming off strong performances and away from teams coming off weak ones, beyond what full-season or multi-year rating would justify.
claimed_edge: An early study of 2264 NFL games from 1981-1995 found bettors overweight outstanding performance over the prior game, prior 2-5 games, and prior season, producing lines that overreact; a 2021 paper, Behavioral biases in the NFL gambling market: Overreaction to news and the recency bias, reports a related, more recent overreaction-to-news effect in the same market.
data_needed: Short-window recent-form metric (last 1-5 games) versus a longer-run team-strength rating, joined to the spread line and ATS outcome, for every game.
skeptic_note: The foundational study uses 1981-1995 data, before modern analytics and line-setting software; the 2021 paper was found through search snippets only and its exact effect size and whether it survives at the closing line (versus opening) could not be confirmed here because the publisher page returned 403 on fetch, so the magnitude claim is unverified pending direct access to the paper.

title: NFL anchoring to preseason Super Bowl odds
mechanism: Bettors form an initial impression of team quality from preseason Super Bowl futures odds and keep anchoring weekly in-season bets to that first impression rather than fully updating on each weeks new information, so teams priced well in the preseason keep attracting betting support (and arguably favourable treatment in weekly lines) deeper into the season than current form justifies.
claimed_edge: A 2025 Economics Letters paper, Anchoring bias in the NFL gambling market, reports bettors prefer teams with better preseason Super Bowl odds throughout the season, and finds a significant relationship between preseason odds and bettor profitability specifically in weeks 2 through 8, with sportsbooks not fully arbitraging the bias out of closing lines.
data_needed: Preseason Super Bowl futures odds for every team and season, joined to each teams weekly closing moneyline/spread and game outcome through roughly week 8.
skeptic_note: Fetch of the ScienceDirect page returned 403, so this summary relies on search-result snippets rather than the full paper; the exact edge size and sample years are unverified, and preseason futures odds are not a column in any dataset available to this project, so it cannot be tested here regardless.

title: NBA hot/cold streak momentum under-adjustment
mechanism: Bettors and bookmakers treat a teams four-plus game winning or losing streak as noise around its season-long rating (gamblers fallacy-adjacent regression-to-mean assumption) and under-adjust the spread, when streaks in fact carry some real signal about current form (injuries, lineup changes, confidence) that a pure rating misses.
claimed_edge: A Sport Journal study spanning 2001-2013 (roughly 13 seasons, about 32000 team-games) reports betting with four-plus game winning streaks to cover and four-plus game losing streaks to miss the cover produced a 56.5 percent overall ATS win rate, above the approximately 52.4 percent break-even rate, positive in every season studied.
data_needed: Game-by-game NBA results and closing spreads 2001-2013 or later, with rolling win/loss streak length per team, opponent-strength and rest-day controls.
skeptic_note: Camerer (1989, American Economic Review), one of the most cited studies in this literature, using 1983-1986 NBA data, found momentum affects the point spread line itself but the markets pricing error is too small to profitably exploit; a 56.5 percent win rate over 13 full seasons with zero losing seasons is a large, suspiciously clean result relative to that earlier finding and relative to the Vandenbruaene et al. (2022) meta-finding that most published spread-betting edges fail a strict multiple-testing correction, so this specific number should be treated as unverified until it can be reproduced on independent data.

title: NHL totals under/over bias (contested)
mechanism: The NHL was the last major North American league to get deep sportsbook and public betting attention, and goal totals depend heavily on goaltending matchups and pace, both harder for casual bettors and even books to price quickly than NFL/NBA/MLB scoring; the claim is that this slower integration left totals mispriced, with bettors and books leaning toward unders out of habit from lower-scoring eras.
claimed_edge: An earlier, smaller-sample study (Market Efficiency and the NHL totals betting market: Is there an under bias?) found the NHL totals market inefficient with profitable simple strategies; a later dissertation (Traugutt, University of Northern Colorado) using a more expansive closing-total-and-odds dataset and five heuristic-based strategies found the market was largely efficient, with only one of the five strategies producing a marginal above-average return.
data_needed: NHL closing total line, over/under odds, and final combined score for every regular-season game, plus whichever heuristic inputs (e.g. starting goalie save percentage, back-to-back status) each strategy requires.
skeptic_note: The two studies disagree directly, and the more recent, larger-sample one found the earlier inefficiency mostly gone, with only a marginal edge surviving from one of five tested strategies, which is itself close to what multiple-testing noise would produce; no NHL dataset exists in this project to check either claim.

title: Fade the public favourite (Levitt price-to-exploit hypothesis)
mechanism: Levitt (2004) argued sportsbooks do not set prices to balance action on both sides; instead they know bettors systematically overbet favourites (and road favourites) and set prices to exploit that known bias, earning more profit than a balanced book would, since the bias is reliable enough that the book does not need to hedge symmetrically.
claimed_edge: Levitt (2004, The Economic Journal), using NFL bet-level tournament data, found sportsbooks earn roughly 20-30 percent more profit by pricing to exploit bettor favourite-side bias than they would by setting lines to balance the book; follow-up NFL and NBA studies describe this as the price-to-exploit or Levitt hypothesis of sportsbook behaviour.
data_needed: Ticket count or handle percentage by side (not just closing price) alongside the price itself, since the mechanism is about how the book sets price relative to where the public money goes, not about price versus outcome alone.
skeptic_note: A 2026 preprint (The profit-bias identity in sports betting), analyzing 1139 MLB run-line games from May-August 2026, found the exact public pattern Levitt describes (home bet share on favourites swinging from under 25 percent to over 80 percent depending on who is favoured) but no detectable mispricing beyond the standard hold (average shading +0.48 percentage points, p=0.54); book profit (5.20 percent of handle, CI 0.88-9.35 percent) was statistically indistinguishable from the hold alone. This directly contradicts treating the Levitt mechanism as a live, exploitable-by-bettors edge in current closing lines; it may now describe only how the book earns its hold, not an exploitable mispricing, and this preprint is not yet peer reviewed.

title: Public over-bias on player props (value on unders)
mechanism: Recreational bettors prefer to root for a players counting stat to go over a number (more points, yards, strikeouts) rather than under, so sportsbooks anticipate lopsided ticket and handle share toward overs and shade the posted number and odds to balance expected liability. This is the same price-to-exploit logic Paul and Weinbach document for NFL sides and totals: bettor dollars are not split 50/50 by side, and books price to the known bias rather than to balance action. If the shade on a given prop exceeds the true probability shift, the under carries positive expected value net of vig.
claimed_edge: No peer-reviewed study found that measures this directly on player props specifically. A wide, repeated practitioner consensus (multiple independent prop-betting guides) states public ticket and handle counts skew toward overs on player props and that unders carry value when the public is heavily on the over, but none of these sources publish a backtest, hit rate, or sample size for the player-prop case specifically; the hard data behind the mechanism (Paul and Weinbach) is for NFL game sides and totals, not props.
data_needed: Ticket count and handle percentage by side (not just the closing price) for a large sample of player props across NFL/NBA, plus the closing odds and the realized over/under result, to test whether the public-money-to-price relationship Paul and Weinbach find for sides and totals also holds for props, and whether fading the public side beats the vig.
skeptic_note: This is the single most repeated claim in prop-betting content, which is itself a reason for caution: an edge this well publicized for years should already have been priced away by the few books that actually move numbers (Caesars, FanDuel). No source quantifies it on props, only on game totals/sides.

title: Hot-hand recency bias in MLB hitter DFS pricing (illusory, fade it)
mechanism: DFS lineup builders and, by analogy, prop bettors overweight a hitters last few games (a representativeness heuristic) and believe a short hot streak predicts the next games output, even though the streak has no real predictive power; the money that wins fades this belief rather than following it.
claimed_edge: Losak, Weinbach and Paul, Does Smart Money Believe in the Hot Hand? Evidence From Daily Fantasy Baseball (American Behavioral Scientist, first published online 2024, issue 2026, vol 70 no 1 pp 93-110) report no evidence of a real hot-hand effect in MLB hitters and no evidence a hot-hand selection strategy is profitable, but that DFS consumers believe in it and incorporate it into lineup decisions regardless; winning lineups use hot-streak players at a lower rate than losing lineups.
data_needed: Per-hitter rolling recent-performance (hot/cold streak flag over last 3-10 games) joined to either DFS ownership or, for a sportsbook test, hitter prop (hits/total bases) closing line movement, to check whether the number is shaded toward the over after a hot last few games the way DFS ownership is.
skeptic_note: This is DFS salary-cap lineup selection (relative ranking against a slates salary cap), not a calibrated sportsbook probability, so the finding should not be assumed to transfer one-for-one to how a book sets a hits or total-bases prop line; no hitter prop dataset is available to test this directly, and it also only applies to hitters, not pitchers (see the companion finding below).

title: Hot hand is real and underpriced for NBA DFS salaries and MLB starting pitchers
mechanism: Unlike the MLB-hitter case above, two papers from an overlapping set of authors report a genuine short-term form effect that market pricing (DFS salary, which functions like a usage/output price set by the platform rather than a bettor-driven line) does not fully absorb.
claimed_edge: Paul, Weinbach and Losak, Market Efficiency and the Setting of Salaries for NBA Daily Fantasy on FanDuel and DraftKings (Journal of Prediction Markets, Dec 2020, vol 14 no 2 pp 45-60) find NBA DFS salaries under-price a real hot-hand effect: players who exceeded salary-based expectations in recent games continue to outperform salary-based expectations in the next game, rejecting market efficiency in salary-setting. Baris and Losak, Hot Hand Effects: Analyzing MLB Starting Pitchers in Daily Fantasy Sports and Betting Markets (International Journal of Sport Finance, first published online Feb 2026, vol 21 no 1), using a methodology that classifies pitchers as hot, cold or neutral on context-adjusted recent performance, report strong evidence that short-term streaks predict DFS outcomes.
data_needed: For pitchers: a recent-form hot/cold classification independent of whatever mu_model already encodes, joined to p_over_mkt and the realized strikeout count, to see whether the betting market under-adjusts for a pitchers last 2-3 starts the way DFS salary-setting does. For NBA: DFS salary history plus actual output; not present in any dataset we currently have.
skeptic_note: This directly contradicts the MLB-hitter hot-hand entry above, from two of the same three authors, in a different population (pitchers, not hitters) and a different market (NBA DFS salaries, not bettor-set lines). Hot hand effects here look real for some player/stat combinations and illusory (and already a belief, not a price, error) for others; it does not generalize. This agent could not access the full Baris and Losak text (paywalled past the abstract) to confirm whether the pitcher streak effect is shown against sportsbook strikeout-prop closing lines specifically, or only against DFS salaries/outcomes.

title: MLB strikeout props lag matchup whiff-rate, platoon split and umpire factors
mechanism: Books post strikeout lines well before first pitch, built mainly off a pitchers season and last-3-to-5-start K rate; practitioner sources claim the market under-weights pitch-level whiff/Stuff+ divergence, the opposing lineups platoon-split strikeout rate, and the home-plate umpires called-strike-zone tendency, so the true expectation can sit further from the posted number than the price reflects.
claimed_edge: Multiple independent strikeout-prop betting guides (heatcheckhq, proprstats, oddsshopper, tonyspicks) describe this as the strongest long-term pitcher-prop market for exactly this reason, but none of them publish a backtest, win rate, or sample size; it is an unsupported, if widely repeated, claim.
data_needed: Already closely matched by the mlb_k_props dataset (mu_model, p_over_model, p_over_mkt, ump_k_factor, park_k_factor, league_k, expected_bf): the test is simply whether p_over_model beats p_over_mkt against the realized strikeout count, i.e. whether a model that already encodes umpire and park K factors has any edge over the posted market price.
skeptic_note: The claim as stated by practitioners is generic enough (pitch mix, umpire, matchup) to be unfalsifiable in blog form. The mlb_k_props dataset already ships ump_k_factor and park_k_factor as columns, meaning whoever built mu_model already tried to price these in; the open question is whether mu_model beats p_over_mkt at all, not whether these factors matter in principle. Topic T03 (pending) is specifically scoped to MLB pitcher-prop modelling and may supersede this entry with a more precise mechanism.

title: MLB strikeout overs overpriced on short rest or heavy recent workload
mechanism: A pitcher on short rest or coming off an unusually high pitch count in his last start may lose stuff/velocity, get pulled earlier for fewer batters faced, or both; if the posted strikeout line anchors mainly to season and trailing K rate rather than to rest days and recent workload jointly, the over should be priced too generously in these specific starts and fade-able.
claimed_edge: A cluster of practitioner betting-strategy pages (cleatz bullpen fatigue, coresportsbetting tired bullpens, heatcheckhq strikeout strategy) assert that short rest and heavy recent pitch counts create a fade opportunity on strikeout overs; one page (innovativecrystals) attached specific run-differential numbers to a related pitch-count claim but, on inspection, those numbers had no cited source, methodology, sample size or time period, so this agent is excluding them as unverifiable rather than repeating them.
data_needed: Already present in mlb_k_props as rest_days, pitches_last3, tr_bf and expected_bf alongside p_over_model and p_over_mkt: the test is whether the gap between p_over_model/realized strikeouts and p_over_mkt correlates specifically with short rest_days or high pitches_last3, rather than being flat across workload levels.
skeptic_note: No source provides a real backtest, hit rate or sample size for this specific angle; one candidate source presented numbers that this agent could not verify and believes were fabricated or unsourced. Modern MLB teams script pitch counts and have detailed internal workload models (Pitch Smart guidelines), so it is plausible teams and books both already account for this, leaving little or nothing for a bettor to find.

title: Secondary and low-volume player props carry no market-maker and stale season-average pricing
mechanism: A sportsbook posts hundreds of player props per slate and cannot apply sharp, matchup-adjusted modelling to every one of them the way it does to the handful of game sides and totals; secondary/bench-player and exotic props get lower limits and are set largely off season-long averages rather than current role, recent usage, or matchup, and there is no single sharp price-setting book for props the way Pinnacle/Circa act for sides, so a stale number can persist longer before any sharp action corrects it.
claimed_edge: Consistent across many independent practitioner sources (wizardofodds, oddsshopper, topendsports, betstamp, establishtherun): spreads/totals hold around 4.5-5%, major star-player props run roughly 4-6%, secondary/bench props roughly 6-10%, and exotic/live props 10-20%+; establishtherun separately reports that even the two most efficient US books for NFL props (Caesars, FanDuel) are not true market-makers the way Pinnacle/Circa are for sides, and that Pinnacle/Betcris/Circa post only a limited, late prop sheet. None of these sources publish a profitability backtest; the hold numbers are observable facts, the inference that the extra hold is exceeded by mispricing is a claim.
data_needed: Player prop lines and closing odds segmented by bet-limit/liquidity tier (star vs bench vs exotic) across multiple books, with the realized outcome, for NBA and NFL, to measure whether the model-vs-market gap actually grows with the hold tier or whether the extra vig simply tracks genuine extra uncertainty.
skeptic_note: Higher hold is also a rational response to genuinely higher variance/uncertainty in bench-player outcomes (role can change start to day), not proof of exploitable mispricing net of that higher vig; no source separates the two explanations with real data.

title: Post-injury usage-cascade window for backup and role-player props
mechanism: When a rotation player or starter is ruled out shortly before or during a game, the minutes, touches, targets or usage that redistribute to teammates (the backup, a wing who slides up a position, the primary ball-handler) are not instantly reflected in those teammates own prop lines; practitioners describe a window of roughly 30-90 minutes where the cascade beneficiaries props are still priced off the old, lower-usage expectation.
claimed_edge: Practitioner sources (fantasyteamadvice NBA prop edge tool, debiso injury/lineup value plays, sportscommand injury-impact guide) describe this window and recommend monitoring injury reports before lines/entries close, framing it as one of the most actionable edges in NBA and NFL props; none of them publish a backtest, hit rate, or measured distribution of how long the window actually lasts or how large the resulting edge is.
data_needed: Timestamped injury/inactive announcements paired with timestamped prop-line snapshots (odds history, not just closing) for every teammate of the ruled-out player, across NBA and NFL, to measure the actual repricing lag and whether a bet placed in that window beats the eventual closing number and the final outcome.
skeptic_note: Public reporting (establishtherun, sportsbookadvisor) also says books now react to injury/beat-reporter news within minutes via live monitoring, and competes directly against the claim of a slow-moving 30-90 minute window; the window has plausibly shrunk over time as books invest more in real-time feeds, and no source dates or re-measures it recently.

title: NFL receiving-yards props anchored to season average over matchup-adjusted projection
mechanism: Receiving yards are the product of a chain of correlated sub-events (targets, catch rate, yards after catch), each with its own variance and its own matchup dependence (opponent yards-allowed to the position, game script, implied team pass volume from the game total/spread); practitioner sources claim the posted number leans more heavily on a receivers trailing season average than on this matchup-specific chain, so extreme matchups (a bad pass defense allowing heavy volume, or a tough shutdown matchup) diverge furthest from the market number.
claimed_edge: Practitioner guides (squawka, oddsshopper, nfl-prop-bets) describe receiving yards as the NFL prop market with the most matchup-driven mispricing for this reason, and note the market is thinner than mainline markets (one comparison cited roughly 40 separate book sources for receiving yards versus about 8 for tackles props, implying more price discovery on receiving yards specifically). No source publishes a backtest, hit rate, or sample size for betting the matchup-adjusted side against the posted number.
data_needed: Weekly receiving-yards prop lines (opening and closing) per receiver, opponent pass-defense yards-allowed-to-position splits, team implied pass volume from the closing spread/total, and the realized receiving yards, to build and test a matchup-adjusted projection against the posted number.
skeptic_note: No player-prop dataset for the NFL exists in our current data (only nfl_spread/nfl_total/nfl_moneyline at the game level), so this cannot be tested without new data; a separate web search produced a specific over-projection figure attributed to one study, which this agent could not verify by opening any real source and is explicitly not repeating here as it may be fabricated by the search summarizer rather than drawn from an actual study.

title: Soccer shots-on-target and cards props mispriced by tactical role and low attention
mechanism: Shots-on-target lines reportedly price off season-long shot volume rather than a players current tactical role (a deep-lying midfielder redeployed and rarely entering the final third gets a line still built on an earlier, more advanced role); cards props depend heavily on referee tendency and game-state/rivalry context that is harder to encode than shot volume; both markets get far less public betting attention than headline goalscorer props, which practitioners claim leaves less sharp correction.
claimed_edge: Practitioner sources (tipstercompetition shots-on-target guide, shurzy soccer specialty markets explainer, nationalaccordnewspaper most-mispriced-markets piece) make this claim; none publish a backtest, hit rate, or sample size, and the goalscorer-vs-shots-on-target attention comparison is asserted rather than measured.
data_needed: Player-level xShots/expected-shots data by role and match, team tactical/role-change tracking (e.g. position heatmap shifts), referee card-rate history, matched to shots-on-target and cards prop lines and outcomes; none of this exists in our current datasets (soccer is not one of our schema-covered sports).
skeptic_note: This is the thinnest evidence base of any entry in this batch: three blog posts with overlapping, generic claims and zero data shown. xG/shot models are now widely available and heavily used by public bettors and media (not just sharp shops), which cuts against the low-attention argument for shots-on-target specifically, even if it may still hold for cards.

title: Catcher framing shifts K/BB props independent of pitcher skill
mechanism: Pitch framing by the catcher converts borderline would-be-balls into called strikes and vice versa for poor framers, systematically raising a batterys strikeout rate and lowering its walk rate independent of the pitchers own skill. This is a catcher-level effect not captured by a pitchers trailing rate stats, which average over whichever catchers caught him, so a day with a different-than-usual catcher (backup, platoon partner, call-up) shifts the true expected K and BB away from what the pitchers season rate implies.
claimed_edge: Framing researchers (Dan Turkenkopf 2008, Bill Letson 2010, Marchi and Fast 2011, later formalized in a hierarchical Bayesian model published in the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports) converge on roughly 0.13 runs of value per extra strike stolen, translating to elite framers worth about plus 10 to plus 18 runs a season. No source quantifies this directly in strikeout or walk count terms per start, and no source backtests a catcher-aware adjustment against actual K or BB prop lines.
data_needed: Per-start catcher identity (who actually caught, not just the scheduled starter) and that catchers current-season framing runs or called-strikes-above-average, joined to the pitchers own K and BB rates, the posted strikeout or walk prop line, and realized counts, to test whether games with an unusually good or bad framer behind the plate diverge from the pitchers season-average-implied line more than games with his typical catcher.
skeptic_note: The framing-value numbers are robust and repeatedly replicated, but that is a measure of run value, not of strikeout or walk counts, and no source has translated it into a per-start K or BB prop edge or tested it against real lines. Teams and some books may already have full Statcast framing data and could be pricing starting catcher into the number already, which would leave nothing for a bettor relying on public framing stats alone.

title: Umpire deference to star batters skews K and BB beyond a flat umpire factor
mechanism: Human ball-strike umpires may give more favorable borderline calls to recognizable, high-status hitters, not just a generic per-umpire zone-size tendency, so a lineup stacked with stars should see fewer called strikeouts and more walks against it than a flat per-umpire or per-batter-handedness factor would predict, with the gap shrinking or vanishing once calls are automated.
claimed_edge: Song, Kang and Paulsen, Technology adoption and bias in officiating: automated Ball-Strike System implementation in Korean Baseball, European Sport Management Quarterly, published online 9 Jul 2026, use 2023-2024 KBO difference-in-differences data (n=148 batters, n=112 pitchers) around the KBO 2024 full ABS adoption and find ABS significantly lowered OBP, IsoD, BB percent and raised SO percent for high-status batters relative to low-status batters, reported as roughly 3 more strikeouts and 2 fewer walks per 100 plate appearances for a famous hitter under human umpires versus ABS. No equivalent effect was found for high-status pitchers.
data_needed: Per-plate-appearance batter identity or fame proxy (All-Star appearances, career WAR, search-interest rank) crossed with the home-plate umpire for each start, to see whether a pitchers realized K and BB against a star-heavy lineup diverges from a model umpire-average-only factor like ump_k_factor. MLB in 2026 still uses full human ball-strike calling with only a limited batter or pitcher challenge system, so this needs MLB-side plate-appearance-level umpire and batter data, not KBO-side.
skeptic_note: This is KBO evidence, a different league and umpire corps, around a 2024 full-ABS cutover, not MLB, where ball-strike calling in 2026 is still entirely human apart from a limited challenge system; whether the same star-deference pattern exists among MLB umpires specifically is untested here. The effect is also measured on batters, with no effect found on pitchers, so it would only matter for the lineup side of a K or BB prop, not the pitchers own identity.

title: Air density changes which pitch-mix pitchers beat the market, not just raw K rate
mechanism: Thin or low-density air from heat, altitude, low pressure or humidity reduces how much a pitch breaks, and pitchers appear to adjust pitch mix in response, throwing relatively more breaking stuff on low-density days. The claim is that sportsbook-implied performance expectations do not fully account for this pitch-mix-by-weather interaction, so comparing realized performance to market-implied expectations, not raw whiff rate, shows breaking-ball-heavy pitchers beating expectations on low-density days and fastball-heavy pitchers beating expectations on high-density days.
claimed_edge: Paul, Filippi, Ackerman and Albright, The Effects of Atmospheric Conditions on Pitchers, presented at the 2014 MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference, report pitchers who threw a high percentage of breaking pitches outperformed betting-market expectations on low-air-density days, and fastball-heavy pitchers outperformed expectations on high-air-density days. No specific effect size or sample period was available in what this agent could access; findings are drawn from the Syracuse University Falk College summary of the work, not the original slides or paper text.
data_needed: Per-start pitch-type usage percent (breaking versus fastball mix, for example from Statcast), air density computed from temperature, humidity, barometric pressure and altitude at game time, and a betting-market-implied expectation, joined to realized performance, to test the pitch-mix-by-density interaction specifically.
skeptic_note: mlb_k_props already has temp_f, wind_mph, venue and park_k_factor, which would let a test of the plain weather-versus-model-gap main effect run today, but the papers actual claim is an interaction with each pitchers breaking-ball usage rate, and that pitch-mix column does not exist in our data, so the claim as stated is not testable without adding it. This also appears to run against the more intuitive Coors Field finding, that thin air suppresses breaking-ball movement and whiffs, which would hurt breaking-ball pitchers rather than help them beat expectations; the two claims point in opposite directions and should not both be assumed true.

title: Hits-allowed lines anchor to BABIP-driven recent trend instead of regressing to the mean
mechanism: A pitchers batting-average-on-balls-in-play (BABIP) is driven mostly by defense and luck and reverts toward a league or park mean far faster than his strikeout or walk rate does, per DIPS theory. If a hits-allowed prop line is set mainly off recent ERA or hits-allowed trend rather than explicitly regressing recent BABIP to the mean, the number should lag the reversion, leaving unders live after a run of unlucky high-BABIP starts and overs live after a run of lucky low-BABIP starts.
claimed_edge: Voros McCrackens original DIPS analysis (1999-2001, popularized via Baseball Prospectus) and the sabermetric literature that followed, formalized into FIP, xFIP and SIERA, repeatedly show year-to-year and start-to-start BABIP has much lower persistence than K rate, BB rate or HR rate. No source found here quantifies a specific hits-allowed prop win rate or ROI from exploiting this, only the underlying BABIP-persistence fact.
data_needed: A hits-allowed prop line and odds, not present in any current dataset since mlb_k_props covers strikeouts only, the pitchers trailing BABIP-against over a short window of 1 to 3 starts, the league and park average BABIP to regress toward, and realized hits allowed, to test whether fading recent BABIP-driven streaks beats the posted hits-allowed number.
skeptic_note: The BABIP-persistence fact itself is about as well established as anything in sabermetrics and has been public for over 25 years, which cuts against it being a live, unexploited edge, since every team and most modeling books almost certainly already regress BABIP in house. No hits-allowed market exists in our current datasets at all, so this cannot be tested without acquiring new data regardless of whether the edge is real.

title: Trailing batters-faced projections lag the shrinking starter workload trend
mechanism: Strikeouts, walks and hits allowed in a start all scale roughly with batters faced, and the league-wide quick-hook trend of managers pulling starters earlier, especially on a third trip through the order, has been shrinking average starter batters-faced and innings for decades and continues shifting year to year. A projection that weights expected batters faced too heavily toward a pitchers own longer trailing history, rather than the current seasons shorter-leash norm, should systematically overstate batters faced and therefore overstate K, BB and H versus what actually happens.
claimed_edge: FanGraphs and Baseball Prospectus analyses, using real innings and batters-faced data rather than opinion, show batters faced per start by starting pitchers fell from a peak of 30.4 in 1973 to roughly 23.6 by 2017 and to about 22.2 more recently, a decline of several batters a start over the last two decades alone. No source quantifies how much, if any, of this trend remains unpriced in a specific modern prop-pricing model.
data_needed: mlb_k_props already carries both expected_bf, the model batters-faced projection, and tr_bf, trailing or recent batters faced, alongside the realized outcome. The test is whether expected_bf is systematically biased high relative to tr_bf and realized batters faced in a way that correlates with season or month, which is already a fold column, showing the model under-adjusting for the current years shorter-leash norm.
skeptic_note: This predicts a slow, roughly league-wide drift rather than a per-game mispricing, so any detectable effect is likely small relative to game-to-game noise, and may already be absorbed if mu_model re-estimates expected_bf every season rather than using a long multi-year trailing window. Whoever built mu_model may have already handled this, in which case the test should come back null.

title: Hits-allowed models spanning the 2023 shift ban misweight lefty-heavy matchups
mechanism: The 2023 rule banning extreme infield shifts caused a real, measured increase in BABIP and OBP for left-handed hitters, concentrated on line drives and far larger for individual hitters who had previously been shifted against heavily. A hits-allowed or BABIP-based model using a multi-year trailing window that pools pre-ban and post-ban seasons, or that has not reweighted for a specific hitters own pre and post-ban BABIP jump, would understate expected hits for pitchers facing lefty-heavy, previously-heavily-shifted lineups.
claimed_edge: A peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study published in The American Statistician (2026, preprint posted to arXiv Nov 2024), using 2020-2023 panel data with difference-in-differences and player-level synthetic control, finds a league-wide increase of about 9 percentage points in BABIP and OBP for left-handed batters after the ban, with individual effects far larger for specific previously-heavily-shifted hitters; Baseball Prospectus separately reports examples like Corey Seagers BABIP rising from .242 to .291 and Kyle Schwarbers from .240 to .301 after the ban.
data_needed: Hits-allowed prop line and odds, not present in current datasets, batter handedness and a pre-ban shift-rate-against for each hitter a pitcher faces, pitcher BABIP-against windowed strictly post-2023, and realized hits allowed, to test whether a model mixing pre and post-ban eras under or over states hits against lefty-heavy lineups specifically.
skeptic_note: The rule changed in 2023 and it is now 2026, three full seasons later, so any model using even a 2-3 year trailing window is probably already post-ban-only by now, and any mispricing from pooling eras has likely already decayed to nothing. This is really a 2023-2024 edge, not a live 2026 one, and the 9-point figure was corroborated across two independent summaries but should still be reverified against the published abstract text directly before being treated as precise.

title: Pitcher K, BB and H props lag the confirmed-lineup platoon shift
mechanism: Pitcher strikeout, walk and hits-allowed lines reportedly open in the morning off a projected, not yet confirmed, opposing lineup, and the official lineup, which fixes the platoon-handedness mix the pitcher will actually face, does not drop until roughly 2 to 4 hours before first pitch. If a book initial pitcher-prop number is not fully repriced once a materially different-than-projected lineup is confirmed, for example a platoon-disadvantaged regular sitting or two strikeout-prone or patient bats being scratched, the pre-confirmation price should lag the matchup true expectation for a window before first pitch.
claimed_edge: Multiple independent practitioner guides (predictionengine, oddible, thebestbetonsports, propsbot) state K-prop lines typically open 8 to 10am ET off a projected lineup, the official lineup drops 2 to 4 hours before first pitch, and cite related markets, specifically moneylines, moving 6 to 8 cents within 30 minutes of a heavy-platoon lineup posting as evidence books do reprice on confirmation. None of these sources publish a backtest, hit rate or sample size for the pitcher-prop case specifically, and the one concrete repricing-speed number found was for moneylines, not K, BB or H props.
data_needed: Timestamped odds history for pitcher K, BB and H props covering opening line through close, not just the single closing snapshot mlb_k_props provides, paired with the timestamp of official lineup confirmation and the confirmed lineup platoon-handedness composition versus the pre-confirmation projected lineup, to measure whether a bet placed right after confirmation beats the eventual close.
skeptic_note: mlb_k_props only carries a single closing-type line per opportunity with no timestamped odds history, so the core timing claim, whether and when the price moves, cannot be tested with what we have regardless of whether the effect is real. The repricing-speed number this agent found concrete support for was for moneylines reacting to lineups, not pitcher props, so it may not transfer.

title: A real, dated K-prop model backtest nets to breakeven despite a 55 percent win rate
mechanism: This is a refutation entry rather than a mispricing claim: it documents a real, dated, publicly posted track record for a strikeout-prop prediction model and shows a win rate well above 50 percent can still net to roughly zero ROI once true odds and vig are applied. Strikeout props are among the most heavily modeled, publicly scrutinized MLB prop markets, since whiff rate, matchup and park or umpire factors are all publicly available and widely used by both bettors and books, so if any MLB prop market has converged toward efficiency against straightforward modeling approaches, this is the one where it should show up first.
claimed_edge: thecapper.io public MLB strikeout-prop performance page reports a combined record of 160 and 130, a 55.2 percent win rate, across 290 officially graded picks from April 12, 2026 through September 24, 2026, with ROI of negative 0.1 percent, just below the roughly 52.4 to 57 percent breakeven range typical for minus 110 to minus 120 odds.
data_needed: Already essentially matched by mlb_k_props: p_over_model, p_over_mkt, dec_odds or over_odds_american and under_odds_american, and the realized outcome, to compute whether betting p_over_model edge over p_over_mkt at the posted odds would itself net a similarly near-zero ROI, replicating this vendor real-world result on our own data.
skeptic_note: This is one vendor, one model, over about 5.5 months. It is not independent confirmation that every strikeout-prop modeling approach is dead, and 290 picks is a thin sample for pinning down a true ROI near zero to within a percentage point or two either way; backtesting-methodology sources found elsewhere in this project cite a few hundred to over 1,000 bets as the minimum before trusting a win rate. It is nonetheless a real, dated, specific number rather than an unverifiable claim, which is rare enough in this space to be worth recording as the honest baseline to beat.

title: NFL wind suppresses total scoring, underpriced by books
mechanism: Bettors and oddsmakers set the total mainly from team and pace ratings and do not fully discount for wind at the stadium; sustained wind degrades passing efficiency (deep ball accuracy, punt and field goal range) more than the posted total line adjusts for, so realized scoring falls below the total more often than the market price implies.
claimed_edge: Borghesi (Applied Financial Economics 2008), using 1984-2004 NFL seasons, reports a betting strategy using expected weather conditions produces an out-of-sample under win rate significantly above the 52.38 percent break-even threshold. A 2025 practitioner replication across about 7,000 games from 1999-2025 using actual game-time wind found games with wind 15+ mph hit the under 56 percent of the time (56, 58, then 55 percent across three decades) versus 49 percent in calm games, with scoring variance essentially unchanged (13.8 vs 14.1 points standard deviation).
data_needed: Game-time (not pregame-forecast) sustained wind speed in mph at the stadium, closing total line, over and under odds, and final combined score for every outdoor game.
skeptic_note: The practitioner replication explicitly used actual game-time wind rather than the pregame forecast, and states the edge depends on that gap: once wind is forecast and obvious before kickoff, the line-setter has already priced it in. If the wind_mph column in this dataset is a pregame forecast rather than measured in-game wind, the edge could be much smaller or absent. Also note the sibling finding that cold temperature alone did not show a matching edge in the same replication.

title: Cold temperature alone does not push NFL totals under
mechanism: A common bettor and media narrative assumes freezing temperatures suppress scoring the same way wind does, so public money leans toward the under in cold games. If cold has little independent effect on scoring once wind and dome status are separated out, that public lean would not be matched by a real scoring effect, leaving no edge, or a value trap for anyone mechanically fading cold-weather games to the under.
claimed_edge: A practitioner replication across roughly 7,000 NFL games from 1999-2025 found games at 32 degrees Fahrenheit or below hit the under only 47 percent of the time, below the 50 percent coin-flip rate and below the 52.4 percent break-even line for -110 odds, concluding cold has little independent effect on scoring once wind is measured separately.
data_needed: Game-time temperature in degrees Fahrenheit (already present as temp_f), closing total line, and final combined score for every outdoor game.
skeptic_note: This is a single practitioner analysis, not peer reviewed, and does not report a sample size breakdown or confidence interval for the 47 percent figure, so the gap from 50 percent could be noise. Treat this as a caution against the cold-equals-under folk belief rather than as a confirmed edge betting the over in cold games.

title: Rain reduces NFL scoring but cannot be isolated with available data
mechanism: Wet footing and a wet ball increase fumbles and drops and reduce passing efficiency, lowering expected points in a way similar to wind. If the market under-weights rain the way Borghesi found for wind and heat, unders would be profitable in rain games, but testing this requires knowing whether and how hard it rained at kickoff.
claimed_edge: Borghesi (Applied Financial Economics 2008, 1984-2004 NFL seasons) reports that heat, wind, and rain each reduce point production and that the market does not fully incorporate these effects into the total line, but the available abstract and excerpts do not break out a rain-only win rate or sample size separate from the combined weather strategy.
data_needed: A precipitation or rain indicator at kickoff (binary flag or rate), which is not present in nfl_total; that dataset carries temp_f and wind_mph but no precipitation column.
skeptic_note: Cannot be isolated from the combined wind, rain, and heat strategy Borghesi reports without a rain variable. The cold-temperature refutation above shows that one leg of this bundled weather claim did not survive independent replication, so rain specifically should not be assumed to work until tested on its own with real precipitation data.

title: Referee crew identity shifts game totals (contested)
mechanism: Individual officiating crews differ in how aggressively they call holding, defensive holding, and other discretionary penalties. A crew calling more offensive penalties kills drives and suppresses scoring toward the under, while one calling more defensive penalties (especially pass interference or defensive holding) extends drives and pushes scoring toward the over. If these tendencies are stable from year to year, totals could in principle be shaded by assigned crew before the public catches on.
claimed_edge: Practitioner trackers report individual crew over and under rates that look large (one crew around 70 percent over, another around 75 percent under across multi-year windows), but a panel study of NFL officiating using 2009-2022 data found crew-level home-bias correlation across seasons of only -0.04, statistically indistinguishable from no stable crew identity effect.
data_needed: An assigned referee or crew identifier for every game, each crew full roster by season (crews are reshuffled), penalty counts by type and team, closing total line, and final score.
skeptic_note: No referee or crew identifier exists in nfl_total, nfl_spread, or nfl_moneyline, so this cannot be tested with current data. More importantly, the one academic-style panel study found near-zero cross-season stability, consistent with crew trends being small-sample artifacts that regress once a crew roster changes, which the NFL does periodically. The practitioner over and under percentages quoted above come from unspecified, likely short windows and should be treated skeptically.

title: NFL bye-week rest edge decayed after the 2011 CBA
mechanism: Before the 2011 collective bargaining agreement limited padded and contact practice time, an extra week of rest let a team use additional practice reps to prepare, producing a real on-field edge that the market underpriced. The CBA capped how much of that practice-time advantage bye teams could actually use, shrinking the true edge, but bettors and some line-setters kept pricing the bye team as if the old edge still existed, which would show up as a reversal once the practice-time mechanism went away.
claimed_edge: One practitioner analysis reports teams off a bye covered the spread 56.3 percent of the time (plus 7.6 percent ROI) as roughly half-point favorites on average from 2002-2010, but only 48.9 percent of the time (minus 6.6 percent ROI) from 2011 onward. A separate, longer-window analysis covering 2002-2025 puts the overall bye-team cover rate at 51.7 percent, below the 52.38 percent break-even line, while teams with a 3-6 day rest edge that is not a full bye covered 54.6 percent with a 4.2 percent ROI over 233 games from week 6 onward in the last decade.
data_needed: Rest days for both teams, already present as home_rest_days, away_rest_days, and rest_diff, plus closing spread line and odds and the ATS result, split by season before and after 2011 and by full bye (7+ day gap) versus smaller 3-6 day rest edges.
skeptic_note: These are practitioner backtests, not peer reviewed, and the cited numbers (56.3/48.9 percent pre/post-2011, and 51.7 percent over the full 2002-2025 window) are not fully consistent with each other, which may reflect different underlying filters such as favorite-only versus all bye teams. The 233-game sample for the 3-6 day rest edge is also small enough that a few percentage points of the reported ROI could be noise.

title: Thursday Night Football unders beat the total
mechanism: A short week between a Sunday or Monday game and a Thursday game cuts practice and recovery time roughly in half, limiting offensive game-plan installation, keeping injured players out longer, and increasing fatigue-driven penalties such as false starts and holding that stall drives, all of which should push realized scoring below a total line that is not discounted enough for the shortened preparation window.
claimed_edge: One tracker reports Thursday Night Football games from 2019-2024 (six seasons) went under the total at a 53.2 percent rate (over rate 46.8 percent). A separate, smaller sample of 48 TNF games since 2019 put unders at 60.1 percent (98-65 combined across other reported seasons) or 60.4 percent in a 19-over/29-under split. Practitioner consensus across multiple sites agrees the under is the most consistently cited TNF angle, generally quoted in the 53-55 percent range.
data_needed: Game day of week, or rest days of 4 or fewer for at least one team as a proxy for a short week, plus closing total line, over and under odds, and final combined score.
skeptic_note: Reported hit rates vary widely across sources, from 53.2 to 60.4 percent, depending on the sample window and what counts as a qualifying game, which suggests the headline number is sensitive to the chosen endpoints. One source notes the market has tightened pricing on this exact angle in recent seasons, and at a sample of 48 to 96 games the confidence interval around any of these estimates is wide enough to include break-even.

title: NFL travel and jet-lag spread edge (likely refuted)
mechanism: The claim is that crossing time zones, especially traveling west to east, disrupts circadian rhythm and hurts visiting-team performance beyond a generic road-travel adjustment, so a market pricing only standard home-field advantage would misprice games with a jet-lagged visitor, or conversely overprice the effect once it becomes a well-publicized betting trend such as fading Pacific-time-zone road teams.
claimed_edge: Borghesi (1981-2004 NFL seasons) found westward time-zone crossings significantly raise home-team win probability, with the effect increasing with travel distance at a decreasing rate, and reported the pointspread market, though not the totals market, could be profitably exploited. A later replication (medRxiv 2023, American Journal of Epidemiology 2025) using nine college football seasons from 2013-2022 excluding 2020 (6,245 games) and a causal-inference design found jet-lag effects compatible with the null hypothesis (P = .133), and explicitly re-ran two prior studies claiming a profitable NFL jet-lag betting effect without finding a significant result in replication.
data_needed: Home and away team travel distance and time zones crossed per game, derivable from a static team-city lookup joined to the home and away team codes but not itself a column in nfl_spread, plus the closing spread and ATS result.
skeptic_note: This is a direct peer-reviewed refutation, not just decay: the more recent and methodologically stronger causal-inference replication explicitly tested and rejected the earlier NFL jet-lag betting claims. Treat the original Borghesi finding as superseded rather than as a live edge. Also not testable here since nfl_spread has no travel-distance or time-zone column, only team codes.

title: Backup QB insertion mispriced by the market (timing edge)
mechanism: When a starting quarterback is ruled out, the spread can swing 3 to 7 points within minutes of the news, and sportsbooks reportedly start shading the line as soon as a starter misses Wednesday or Thursday practice, before the official injury-report tag appears. If sportsbooks anchor the backup discount to a historical average starter-to-backup talent gap rather than the actual ability of that particular backup, the market may be correct in direction but wrong in magnitude, leaving value on one side once the line settles.
claimed_edge: A sportsbook-side source (a Caesars Sportsbook head of football) stated that undervaluing backups was one of the lessons of a recent season, and one tracker reported backup starters at a combined 7-4 straight up in-season, framed as evidence the market overcorrects against backup-led teams. No peer-reviewed study or systematic practitioner backtest reporting a win rate and sample size was found quantifying this specific mispricing.
data_needed: Timestamped injury-report status changes and timestamped line movement (full open-to-close odds history, not just a closing snapshot) for every game with a QB change, plus a measure of backup QB quality independent of the small-sample game log that produces the discount in the first place.
skeptic_note: Every source here is a sportsbook anecdote, a single-season small-sample record (7-4), or a qualitative claim about line-movement timing; none report a multi-season win rate or ROI. The nfl_spread and nfl_moneyline datasets only carry a single closing snapshot (home_starter plus qb_epa, attempts, and career_games as of that game) with no timestamped pre-injury line, so the actual claim, that the market misprices in the hours after injury news, cannot be tested with this data at all.

title: NFL spread market prices the 3 and 7 key numbers correctly (limited edge)
mechanism: NFL margins of victory cluster heavily at 3 (one field goal) and 7 (touchdown plus extra point) because of how the sport scores. If sportsbooks under-shade the odds when a spread sits exactly on or crosses one of these numbers, bettors could extract value by betting into or buying off the number; conversely, if books already widen the vig around these numbers, as is standard industry practice, the historical clustering is already priced in and not exploitable.
claimed_edge: The 3-point margin occurs in roughly 14.4 percent of games in 2015-2019 data, cited elsewhere as 15.1 percent over a longer run, with 7 the second most common margin at roughly 9 percent. Dare and Holland (2004) tested home-underdog and several other spread betting rules against this distribution and found home underdogs performed better than naive expectation but the profit was not statistically significant, with nine other tested rules performing worse. Industry pricing sources state sportsbooks now commonly charge roughly -120 or worse, versus a standard -110, on half-point lines crossing 3 or 7, reflecting awareness of the clustering.
data_needed: Closing spread_line together with home and away spread odds, to see the actual vig charged at and around 3 and 7, and the ATS outcome; already present in nfl_spread as spread_line, home_spread_odds, away_spread_odds, plus the hidden won/push outcome.
skeptic_note: Dare and Holland explicitly found the one rule closest to this effect, home underdogs, was not statistically significant, and the broader academic consensus across this topic is that the NFL spread market is close to efficient. This entry is really a test of whether this dataset spread_line and odds pairing already reflects known key-number pricing, a sanity check on market sophistication, rather than a believable new source of profit.

title: NFL total-score clustering at 41, 43, 44, 47 (structural, not obviously exploitable)
mechanism: Like spread margins, final combined scores cluster at numbers reachable by common combinations of field goals and touchdowns, with 41, 43, 44, and 47 the most frequent game totals. If sportsbooks post total lines at or near these numbers without enough extra vig, the push risk and true win probability at that exact number would be mispriced the same way key spread numbers can be.
claimed_edge: 2004-2013 data put the frequency of final totals at 41, 43, 44, and 47 at 3.9, 3.7, 4.1, and 3.2 percent respectively. A longer 2000-2026 sample shows 44 at 3.85 percent, 41 at 3.81 percent, 43 at 3.48 percent, and 47 at 3.16 percent, with a reported shift since 2015 in which 44 fell from the single most common total to roughly the tenth most common, implying the clustering itself is not stationary over time.
data_needed: Closing total_line together with over and under odds, to see the vig charged at these specific numbers, and the final combined score; already present in nfl_total as total_line, over_odds, under_odds, plus the hidden won/push outcome.
skeptic_note: No source found tests whether sportsbooks actually underprice vig at these specific total numbers; unlike the spread key-number case, no Dare-and-Holland-style formal academic test turned up for totals. The finding that 44 dropped sharply in rank after 2015 is itself evidence the clustering drifts as rule changes, kicking distance, and pace shift the scoring environment over time, so a strategy tuned to 2004-2013 frequencies could already be stale against 2020s data.

title: NBA back-to-back rest penalty is mostly already in the closing spread
mechanism: A team playing on zero days of rest shows measurable in-game decline (worse shooting, fewer rebounds), so if the market under-shades the spread for this, the rested team would be backable; but the same analysis that measures the effect derives it from, not hides it from, the existing line.
claimed_edge: An inpredictable.com CART (classification and regression tree) analysis of 2003-2010 NBA games (7848 games) found a team playing with zero days rest is penalized roughly 0.75 to 1.25 points in the point spread (the author revised the estimate from 0.75 to 1.25 points), implying NBA true home-court advantage is closer to 3.25 points once rest is isolated from the raw 3.5-point home constant. Only the immediate prior-game rest variable (rest1) was predictive; deeper patterns such as 2-games-in-3-nights or 3-in-4 added nothing once rest1 was in the model. Road teams landed on back-to-backs about 4x more often than home teams in this sample (1887 vs 485 team-games).
data_needed: Per-game days of rest for home and away teams, closing spread line and spread odds, and the ATS result; no NBA dataset currently exists in this project.
skeptic_note: This is explicitly a study of what the rest variable already explains inside the observed line (a residual-line regression), not a claim that the market fails to price it; the author frames it as explaining the spread, not beating it. The sample (2003-2010) predates the load-management era reduction in back-to-backs per team, so the magnitude may no longer match current scheduling.

title: Eastward jet lag hurts the traveling home team in the NBA
mechanism: Circadian misalignment from recent eastward travel degrades a NBA team shooting, rebounding, and win probability even when that team is playing at home (returning from a western road trip to host a game), so a market that only prices generic rest or a visiting-team travel penalty would miss this direction-specific, home-team-own-travel effect.
claimed_edge: A peer-reviewed study (PMC9245584) of 11481 NBA regular-season games across 30 teams, 2011-12 through 2020-21 seasons, found home teams playing under eastward jet lag had winning percentage down 6.03 percent (p = 0.051) and point differential down 1.29 points (p = 0.015) versus home teams with no jet lag; a 2-hour eastward shift produced a 4.53 point differential drop (p < 0.05) and a 1-hour shift a 0.72 point drop (p = 0.07); rebound differential fell 1.29 (p < 0.0001) and effective field goal percentage fell 1.2 percent (p < 0.01). Westward jet lag showed no significant effect for home or away teams, and away teams showed no significant directional jet lag effect either direction.
data_needed: Per-game time-zone-crossing history for the home team over the prior several days (to classify eastward vs westward jet lag and magnitude), season/date, and closing spread line, odds, and ATS result; no NBA dataset currently exists in this project.
skeptic_note: Several of the component p-values sit right at or just above 0.05 (0.051, 0.07) across multiple tested directions and magnitudes, which is consistent with some selective significance across a multi-way test; the study measures raw outcomes, not whether this is already reflected in betting lines, so whether it survives against a market that already shades generically for travel and rest is untested by this paper.

title: Denver and Utah altitude home advantage exceeds a generic home-court constant
mechanism: Visiting teams, unacclimated to mile-high elevation, suffer disproportionate cardiovascular fatigue in a running sport, giving Denver (and Utah, also high-altitude) a larger true home edge than a single league-wide home-court number would predict; if the market applies one average home-court adjustment rather than a team-specific altitude premium, lines in Denver and Utah would be too generous to the visitor.
claimed_edge: Lopez, Matthews and Baumer (arXiv:1701.05976), using Bayesian state-space models fit to roughly a decade of betting-market data across NFL, NHL, NBA and MLB, found Denver had the largest team-specific home advantage in the NBA; secondary press coverage (Forbes, Westword) paraphrased this as roughly 67 percent win probability at home against an equal-ability opponent, worth an estimated 2.5 extra wins per season versus the leagues worst (Brooklyn), with Utah showing a similarly outsized edge.
data_needed: Team identity (Denver/Utah flag), closing spread line, and a model-implied fair home-court baseline to compare against, plus visiting-team days since last game at elevation; no NBA dataset currently exists in this project.
skeptic_note: The paper itself, per Forbes own description, does not isolate altitude as the specific cause versus travel fatigue, crowd effects, referee bias, or territoriality, so attributing the edge to altitude specifically is a popular-press simplification, not the paper authors own causal claim. This is also an extremely well-known, decades-old, publicly discussed effect (the NBA itself has reportedly discussed schedule changes to blunt it), which is close to the textbook case of something already fully priced into Denver and Utah lines rather than a live edge.

title: NBA referees favor the home team and the team currently trailing (make-up calls)
mechanism: Referees subconsciously, or as an institutional incentive aligned with league revenue, favor the home team, the team currently behind in the game (make-up calls), and the team trailing in a playoff series, all of which shrink margins and extend series; the authors argue all three biases are plausibly profit-enhancing for the league itself, since closer games and longer series generate more attention and revenue.
claimed_edge: Price, Remer and Stone (2012, Journal of Economics and Management Strategy, 21(1), 271-300) tested three hypotheses on NBA officiating and found supporting evidence for all three: home-team bias, in-game trailing-team bias, and series-trailing-team bias.
data_needed: Play-by-play foul calls with game-clock and score context (who is trailing, by how much, when in the game and series) joined to officiating crew identity; far beyond a closing-line schema and not present in any dataset here.
skeptic_note: A direct, later refutation exists: Deutscher (2015, Journal of Sports Analytics, No referee bias in the NBA: new evidence with leagues assessment data) used the NBA own official referee accuracy and assessment data rather than publicly coded video, and the title itself states no bias was found, directly contradicting Price, Remer and Stone. Both the sciencedirect and sagepub full texts for Deutscher were paywalled (403) during this research, so only the title and abstract-level claim could be confirmed, not the exact numbers; still, a published direct rebuttal using better, official (non-public) data is strong reason to treat the original claim as contested rather than settled.

title: Referee call accuracy varies with how close the pregame betting spread is
mechanism: Since the NBA publishes public Last Two Minute officiating-accuracy reports for close games and the league now partners directly with sportsbooks, referees may (consciously or not) make fewer errors in games the market itself has already priced as close contests, meaning officiating quality correlates with the pregame betting spread rather than only with the live score.
claimed_edge: Belasen, Belasen and Olbrecht (2025, Journal of Sports Economics; SSRN working paper 5135514) report that as the pregame betting gap between favorite and underdog narrows, referees make fewer incorrect calls (per Last Two Minute reports) favoring the favorite over the underdog, with a search-engine summary of the abstract citing 23 percent fewer incorrect calls against visiting underdogs and 42 percent fewer against home underdogs in narrow-spread games versus wide-spread games.
data_needed: Per-game Last Two Minute report error counts by team, pregame closing spread line, and officiating crew identity; not present in any dataset here and not something this project has an NBA source for at all.
skeptic_note: Both the SSRN and SAGE full texts returned 403 Forbidden during this research, so the 23 percent and 42 percent figures come from a search-engine summary of the abstract, not text I personally verified; treat those exact numbers as unconfirmed pending direct access. Even if accurate, the paper measures officiating error rate inside the Last Two Minute window specifically, not a demonstrated bettable margin or total effect, so translating it into a trading strategy is not shown by the paper itself.

title: Bet the under on the highest NBA totals (refuted on replication)
mechanism: The public overreacts to recent high-scoring pace and pushes the highest posted totals too high relative to true expected scoring, producing a public-bias overlay that the market does not fully correct for, which should be exploitable by fading (betting under) the highest-posted game totals.
claimed_edge: Paul, Weinbach and Wilson (2004, Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance) tested NBA totals from the 1995-96 through 2001-02 seasons and reported betting the under on high totals was profitable, with win percentages above the roughly 52.4 percent break-even threshold for several of the highest total bins.
data_needed: NBA closing total line, over and under odds, and the final combined score; no NBA dataset currently exists in this project.
skeptic_note: Directly refuted on replication, not just decayed: a follow-up study (The Sport Journal, NBA Gambling Inefficiencies: A Second Look) using 2000-01 through 2007-08 data, the period immediately after the original study, found no statistically significant edge either direction, and I personally fetched and confirmed this full text. Descriptively the pattern even flipped: overs on totals of 211-220 won above 52.38 percent in 8 of 10 cases in the follow-up sample, which the follow-up authors themselves call the opposite of the 2004 study, though they note the log-likelihood ratio never reached significance in either direction. Do not treat the original studys win percentage as a current number.

title: Cross-sportsbook latency after official NBA injury-report status changes
mechanism: Official NBA injury reports update on a scheduled, batch cadence rather than continuously, and different sportsbooks re-price their player-prop and total lines at different speeds once a status change becomes public, so a bettor monitoring the official report and several books at once can act in the gap before the slowest books catch up.
claimed_edge: Practitioner sites describe a roughly 5 to 15 minute lag window on significant status-change news between market-setting sportsbooks and slower-moving recreational-facing books, and generically describe totals moving several points once a star player is confirmed out. No practitioner source found reports an actual realized win rate, ROI, or sample size from trading this specific gap; these are process descriptions, not records.
data_needed: Timestamped (not just closing) odds across multiple sportsbooks and timestamped official injury-report status changes, to measure the realized book-to-book reaction-speed gap and whether it clears the vig on both legs; not present in any dataset here.
skeptic_note: Claim-grade only: no backtest, record, or academic study quantifying this specific latency gap or its profitability was found. Separately, a real 2025 federal gambling case (Terry Rozier, Damon Jones and Chauncey Billups indictments) shows the underlying information-asymmetry mechanism is strong enough that insiders profited illegally from nonpublic injury and minutes information well before any public report, which is suggestive the public-information version of this edge could be real too, but the prosecution itself is evidence only for the illegal, nonpublic version, not this legal public-latency strategy, and the NBA resulting 2025-26 policy changes (fixed report windows, 15-minute update cadence, prop-bet limits) are specifically designed to shrink whatever edge previously existed here.

title: NBA totals lag league-wide or team-specific pace shifts
mechanism: Total points equal possessions multiplied by points-per-possession; if the market anchors total lines mostly to recent scoring averages rather than updating quickly to current pace trends (a league-wide pace increase, or a specific team pace change after a trade or coaching change), lines could lag true expected pace and expected total scoring.
claimed_edge: Practitioner analytics sites report league-wide pace climbing to roughly 104.5 possessions per game in the 2025-26 season from about 102.7 the season before, and assert a 10-possession gap translates to roughly 20 points of expected combined scoring. None of these sources report an actual backtested win rate or sample size from trading a pace lag against the market total line; these are descriptive analytics claims, not records.
data_needed: Team-level rolling pace (possessions per 48 minutes) updated through the current season, the closing total line and odds, and the final combined score; no NBA dataset currently exists in this project.
skeptic_note: Wide claim-grade only: no study found tests whether the market actually lags pace specifically as opposed to being efficient on totals generally, and this has the same big-number-no-sample-size pattern flagged as a risk in the standing orders. Pace is also one of the most heavily tracked public analytics stats in basketball (every major stats site publishes it daily), which argues against the market lagging it for long once a trend is a few games old.

title: NBA referee crew tendencies may lag into totals during the pregame assignment window
mechanism: NBA referee crews are publicly assigned and posted hours before tip-off, and individual crews have historically shown different personal-foul and free-throw-attempt rates; if the total line does not fully re-shade once a particular high-whistle or low-whistle crew is assigned, the gap between the assignment posting and tip-off is a window where the total could lag crew-specific tendencies.
claimed_edge: I confirmed directly from official.nba.com that referee crew assignments are posted at approximately 9:00am ET each game day, many hours ahead of most games. Practitioner betting-content sites (not academic sources) claim crews vary meaningfully in foul rate and that this can swing combined scoring by roughly three to eight points depending on the crew, and that totals can adjust after daily assignments post, but none of these sites report an actual sample size or realized win rate for trading this gap.
data_needed: Officiating crew identity per game joined to historical crew-specific foul and free-throw-attempt rate, both the morning-of-assignment total line and the closing total line (to see whether any shift happens after the 9am posting), and the final combined score; not present in any dataset here.
skeptic_note: All crew-magnitude numbers here are unsourced practitioner claims. Separately, the peer-reviewed literature on whether NBA referees show any systematic scoring-relevant bias at all is actively disputed (see the home-bias finding and its direct academic refutation elsewhere in this topic), so a claim that crew tendencies specifically move totals, built on top of a contested foundation, should be treated skeptically until a real study ties specific crew assignments to realized total outcomes net of the closing line.

title: Closing line value (CLV) as the standard measure of bettor skill
mechanism: A deep, high limit, low vig closing line, the kind a sharp book such as Pinnacle posts right before a game starts, aggregates essentially all public and professional information available, including late sharp action that only shows up hours or minutes before close. A bettor who systematically gets a better price than that final number, averaged over many bets and sports, must on average be acting on real information the market had not yet folded in when the bet was placed, so that gap, CLV, is argued to convert close to linearly into expected profit precisely because the closing line is the best available estimate of true probability, making it the only loss free way to separate skill from luck bet by bet.
claimed_edge: Joseph Buchdahl reports that over nearly 20,000 bets in his Wisdom of the Crowd soccer betting system, actual profit over turnover of 3.4 percent compares closely to an expected value of 4.0 percent implied by the prices taken, which he describes as well within the bounds of statistical significance.
data_needed: Per bet, the price actually taken plus the closing price for the same selection, across a large number of bets, to compute realized CLV and compare it to realized profit; current datasets store a single closing-ish price per game or prop and no record of any actual bets placed at earlier prices.
skeptic_note: The supporting number is from one practitioner system in one sport (soccer) reported by its own creator, not an independent or peer reviewed source; see the companion entries below showing the same relationship breaking down in NBA moneylines and decaying over time even within soccer against Pinnacle specifically.

title: Positive CLV routinely fails to predict bet level profit in NBA moneylines
mechanism: CLV is a relative measure: it shows a bettor beat the rest of the market to a price, not that the price was good enough to clear the built in sportsbook margin.
