In a market with a thick hold such as NBA moneylines, roughly 4.5 percent, a bettor can beat nearly the whole field to the final number and still be laying a price that nets negative after the vig, because CLV compares the bettor price to the market price, not to the true, no vig probability.
claimed_edge: Karl Whelan, author of Fine Margins: Economics Explains Betting, analyzed 3,670 NBA moneyline games across the 2022-23 through 2024-25 seasons using about 34,944 quotes from roughly 10 sportsbooks, comparing prices up to 24 hours before tip off against the closing median. Sorting bets into CLV deciles, three of the five positive CLV deciles did not, on average, make a profit; the ninth decile carried about 5 percent average CLV but only 0.2 percent profit; only the top decile was reliably profitable, 11.4 percent in the main sample and 16 percent in the 24 hour window sample, while the bottom decile lost about 25 percent.
data_needed: Per bet, timestamped odds at the moment of the bet plus the full odds history through closing across multiple books for the same game, to compute each bet own CLV and realized return; current datasets store only one closing-ish price per game.
skeptic_note: One independent analyst blog, not a peer reviewed journal; covers only NBA moneylines over three recent seasons, so it is unclear whether the same breakdown holds in lower vig markets such as spreads or totals, or in deeper markets such as soccer, where the companion entry above holds up much better on average.

title: Pinnacle closing line predictive reliability has decayed in recent soccer seasons
mechanism: The CLV as skill argument depends on the closing line staying close to true probability over time. If arbitrage bettors increasingly force a benchmark book to move its closing price away from its own best probability estimate to avoid being middled, or if that pricing process has simply gotten noisier, a fixed size CLV measured against that close would predict less and less realized profit as the years pass, with no change in bettor skill required to explain it.
claimed_edge: Jay Pinho (Substack, A View From The Pinnacle) reports that expected value bets priced against Pinnacle closing odds in major European soccer leagues returned 3.5 percent actual ROI versus 4.3 percent expected across 23,418 bets from the 2019-20 season onward, but narrowing to the 2023-24 season onward the gap widens sharply, 1.9 percent actual versus 4.2 percent expected across 6,806 bets; he concludes Pinnacle closing odds no longer act as a reliable predictor over this recent window.
data_needed: A multi season, bet level record of expected value bets priced against one benchmark book closing odds in a single sport and market, with timestamps, to see whether the actual versus expected gap is widening over time; not available here, there is no soccer data and no odds history in any current dataset.
skeptic_note: Single author Substack analysis, not peer reviewed; only one mechanism, arbitrage pressure, is offered and not directly tested against alternatives such as ordinary sampling variance between two differently sized, non overlapping windows.

title: NFL moneyline odds shift predictably through the week, driven by sharp action rather than injury news
mechanism: Sportsbooks continuously update their probability estimate as professional and syndicate money arrives across the week, and that updating process leaves a detectable fingerprint: the direction a price has already moved partway through the week helps predict which way it keeps moving into the close, because it is being pushed by the same informed flow rather than by one off news events such as a Wednesday injury report, which arrive at fixed, predictable times and get priced in quickly rather than gradually.
claimed_edge: Elijah Costa, a Claremont McKenna College senior thesis from 2025, analyzing high frequency NFL moneyline odds data from the 2020 through 2024 seasons, reports significant predictability in the direction odds will shift through the week leading up to kickoff, and attributes this to adjustments by sportsbooks to sharp action rather than to injury news.
data_needed: Multiple timestamped odds snapshots per game across the betting week, ideally hourly, not just a single closing price, plus a timestamped injury report feed to separate news driven from sharp driven moves; nfl_moneyline currently has one closing snapshot and no injury news timestamps.
skeptic_note: Undergraduate senior thesis, not a peer reviewed journal article, from a single institution covering one five season window; predictability of the path a line takes during the week is not the same as a bettor being able to beat the eventual close, since the sharp money that creates the predictable path has typically already moved the price by the time it becomes detectable.

title: Reverse line movement is profitable in one NFL practitioner backtest but refuted in peer reviewed NCAAF totals research
mechanism: Books treat a small pool of professional, well capitalized bettors as far more informative than a much larger pool of recreational ticket volume, so when a side is getting a minority of ticket count but the line still moves in that side favor, reverse line movement, it signals the line setters are responding to presumed sharp money, which should on average be more accurate than the crowd it contradicts.
claimed_edge: A BetLabs based practitioner backtest from Sports Insights reports that since 2003, NFL sides receiving under 40 percent of spread tickets while the line moved toward them went 290-249 against the spread for plus 25.82 units and 4.8 percent ROI overall, and 75-57 for 13.9 percent ROI over the two most recent seasons at the time of writing. Separately, Francisco and Moore, Journal of Economics and Finance, 2019, studying NCAA college football totals from September 2005 through January 2016, conclude that following reverse line movement is not a profitable strategy in that market.
data_needed: Timestamped public bet percentage, ticket share, or handle percentage by side, joined to the line movement timeline for the same game, to flag reverse line movement; no current dataset carries any betting percentage or odds history column.
skeptic_note: The one positive number comes from a vendor blog using its own backtesting tool, not a peer reviewed source, and is NFL spreads specifically; the one peer reviewed test found the opposite result in a different sport and market, NCAAF totals, so profitability looks market specific rather than a general law.

title: Chasing steam moves as a retail bettor captures little or no edge
mechanism: A steam move is, by definition, the point at which many books have already repriced in response to sharp action; the informational edge that caused the move belongs to whoever bet into the earlier, stale number, not to whoever reacts afterward. A retail bettor who only sees the move once it has propagated across tracking services is, by construction, betting into the already corrected price, so the move explains why the line changed but does not hand a late follower the value that caused the change.
claimed_edge: Multiple independent practitioner guides describe steam chasing as unprofitable on its own once execution lag is accounted for, framing it as a signal of where sharp money went rather than a standalone strategy; no rigorous backtest or academic study was found that quantifies the profit, if any, available to a bettor who follows a steam move after the fact.
data_needed: Millisecond to second level, simultaneous odds snapshots across many books, to measure how much of a line total move happens before versus after it would be detectable by an outside tracking service; no dataset in this project has sub day level timestamps at all.
skeptic_note: Every source for this entry is practitioner content, not data; the claim is theoretical, value must be captured before you can see it, and no empirical study, even a non peer reviewed one, was found that actually measured the realized return of a steam following bettor.

title: MLB real time betting line movements overreact and partially reverse, rejecting weak form efficiency
mechanism: If bookmakers and the market adjust prices in reaction to order flow rather than purely to new information, a typical price move will overshoot the eventual fair value and then partially revert, producing measurable negative autocorrelation in successive price changes within the same game, a pattern a trader could in principle exploit if able to react fast enough and cheaply enough.
claimed_edge: Jay Simon, Management Science, 2024, analyzing detailed opening to closing betting line movement from four sportsbooks for 3,681 MLB games, finds forecasts are mostly reliable but exhibit significant negatively autocorrelated changes, rejects weak form market efficiency, and shows forecast quality does not improve monotonically as game time approaches, forecasts made 90 minutes before weekend day games are significantly worse than earlier forecasts for the same game despite more information being available by then.
data_needed: A full sequence of intra game week moneyline odds snapshots per game across multiple books, matching this paper granularity; mlb_k_props has only one strikeout prop line around four hours before first pitch and no moneyline history at all.
skeptic_note: The exploitable strategy claim is about moneyline forecast sequences, not the strikeout prop market this project actually has data for, and the paper reports a statistical rejection of weak form efficiency in the forecasts themselves, not a vig adjusted realized bettor return.

title: Information content of the NFL line increases through the betting week but sentiment driven mispricing persists
mechanism: As more bettors, including professional handicappers, place money across the week, each successive quoted line should embed more of the available information than the one before it, so a forecast encompassing test comparing an early week line to the closing line should find the close subsumes the open if the market processes information efficiently. The same data can still show narrower, sentiment linked biases, for example around nationally popular teams, that survive this general improvement, because sentiment comes from the same growing pool of bettors supposedly making the line more accurate overall.
claimed_edge: Miller and Rapach, Journal of Empirical Finance, 2013, using three sequential prices from 1972 NFL season New York City bookmaking data, an early outlaw line, a Tuesday opening line, and a game time closing line, find the closing line contains information beyond the opening line via forecast encompassing tests, consistent with a reasonably well functioning market, but also find significant pricing inefficiencies tied to sentiment measures, and report that the actual recorded bets of professional gamblers in their data were profitable.
data_needed: A three or more point odds history per game across a single betting week, plus a sentiment proxy such as team popularity, and ideally bettor level records; nfl_spread has one closing line per game and nothing from earlier in the week.
skeptic_note: The underlying data is from a single 1972 New York City bookmaking network, a far smaller, less liquid, non electronic market than today multi book, software priced lines, so how much the close beats the open, and the specific sentiment bias found, may not generalize to the modern market this project models.

title: Opening to closing NFL line movement, not just the closing number, retrodicts divisional winners and flags a home underdog rule
mechanism: If the direction and size of a line move from open to close mostly reflects the same late arriving, informed money that drives reverse line movement, the signed opening to closing difference alone, with no public bet percentage data needed, should carry some of the same signal: teams the market pushed toward across the week are teams the combined information flow came to see as stronger than the line setter first guess.
claimed_edge: Szalkowski and Nelson, an arXiv working paper from 2012, using 2,560 NFL games, all regular and post season games from 2002 through 2011, report the opening to closing line difference retrodicts straight up divisional winners with at least 75 percent accuracy, and separately find home teams covered the spread only 47 percent of the time in their sample, such that a rule of betting home underdogs produced a cumulative 53.5 percent against the spread record, above the 52.38 percent breakeven threshold.
data_needed: The opening line alongside the already available closing line for the same game; nfl_spread currently stores only one spread_line field, described as the closing number, with no opening line column.
skeptic_note: An arXiv preprint, not a peer reviewed publication; the 75 percent divisional winner figure is retrodictive, fit and evaluated on the same 2002-2011 window, over a small number of division races per year, and the profitable home underdog rule overlaps with the already registered late season home underdog bias, Borghesi, entry S003, so part of this may be re finding the same effect through a different lens rather than an independent edge.
